attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: Faithful to the pricing-feasibility core. It combines a historical claim with an unlimited forecast; filing it as a forecast is acceptable. The deception and ROI parts are rightly left out.

contract.note: Fair: support needs proof of impossibility, and contradiction needs a documented counterexample with billing basis and service-level economics. 'Economically feasible' is undefined, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Dated interview in which Gamma's CEO says the company is profitable. This is a company self-claim with no defined measure, no billing terms and no service-level costs, so it does not meet the counterexample rule.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and no documented counterexample shows sustained service-level profit without per-user token billing. Gamma's undefined profitability claim does not settle it, and impossibility cannot be shown empirically. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I think it's inevitable' states certainty, not a hedge, so it is scored as a forecast. No horizon. The aside about the Anthropic/OpenAI enterprise move is a reason he gives, not part of the proposition.

contract.note: Fair plain reading: more than half of AI subscription products move to billing tied to tokens. Rightly separates quotas from token billing and does not count interim flat-rate plans as failure.

evidence.note: GitHub's own dated disclosure that Copilot moved to credit-based usage billing. That is one product family and gives no market denominator.
Preprint dated before the cutoff. It finds usage-quota subscriptions dominant among observable rows, but quotas are not token billing, many rows lack prices, and it does not measure a transition.

reviews.rationale: Undated forecast. The packet has one provider's transition and a study that does not show a majority moving to token billing. Nothing makes the transition impossible either. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'when revenue growth fails to follow' antecedent and the open 'at some point' horizon. The parenthetical and the hedged 'likely' layoffs are rightly excluded.

contract.note: Stretched in the speaker's favour. In context ('one bad earnings call') the forecast means skeptical investor pushback when AI-inflated R&D brings no revenue. The contract counts any clarifying analyst question, and treats 11% revenue growth against 14% R&D growth in a quarter called outstanding as revenue 'failing to follow'.

evidence.note: SAP Q2 2026 call: revenue up 11%, cloud up 24%, operating profit up 9%. That is strong growth, not a clear case of revenue failing to follow costs.

A UBS analyst asks why R&D costs rose faster than headcount and where token costs are booked. The CEO answers that tokens drive it and cites productivity gains. This is a neutral composition question, not clear skeptical pushback.

reviews.rationale: Under a fair reading, the SAP exchange is a cost-composition question in a strong-growth quarter. It is not investors questioning AI spending because revenue failed to follow. The antecedent is not clearly met and no conclusive event is shown. Open horizon, so unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful. It is a present-tense observation: large losses, and a revenue base well below what ongoing Oracle payments would need. The Oracle part compares current revenue with future recurring payments.

contract.note: Calendar 2025 is a reasonable baseline and 'incredibly' is read in its ordinary sense. Future Oracle payments may be compared with current revenue as long as they are not relabelled as 2025 bills, which fits 'on an ongoing basis'.

evidence.note: Leaked statements also reviewed by the FT show a 2025 operating loss of about $20.9B, 160% of revenue. The net loss was about $39B, including a roughly $30B noncash charge.
Sources put 2025 revenue at $13.1B and cash burn at $8B. This sets the revenue baseline and shows substantial losses.

Reported (via WSJ, unconfirmed) $300B deal over about five years from 2027, roughly $60B a year. That is far above current revenue, which supports the 'much more money' part, though the contract terms are not public.
FT-sourced loss excluding noncash items is $8B on about $13B revenue. That qualifies the headline figure but still shows large losses.

reviews.rationale: Even after excluding noncash charges, the 2025 loss was about $8B on about $13B revenue, with an operating loss of about $21B, so the business is heavily unprofitable. Reported Oracle commitments of about $60B a year from 2027 far exceed current revenue. The Oracle part rests on an unconfirmed press report.
